extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers interested in art theory and practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating art that is morally purposeful and widely accessible: emphasises subject-matter, form, social function, and the artist's life conditions according to Tolstoy's theory. Useful for writers, composers, and visual artists aiming for simple, clear, and socially unifying work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / universality of artistic activity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Artistic activity will then be accessible to all men... the art of the future... will become accessible to the whole people.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should be produced by gifted members of the whole people rather than confined to upper classes or their hangers-on. Elementary education should include music and drawing so everyone can discover and perfect artistic capacities. The diffusion of good art and examples among the people will serve as the best schools of technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique defined as clearness, simplicity, and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not only will that complex technique ... not be demanded, but, on the contrary, the demand will be for clearness, simplicity, and brevity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Technique’ should be understood as the ability to transmit feeling briefly, simply, and clearly rather than mastery of complicated refinements. These qualities are learned by education of taste and by examples of good art (including peasant art), not merely by mechanical exercises in specialised schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter: feelings that draw men towards union (Christian perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The only subject-matter of the art of the future will be either feelings drawing men towards union, or such as already unite them... the religious perception of our times, Christian feelings, are infinitely new and varied.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's content should express feelings open to all—brotherhood, love, unity—rather than exclusive feelings (pride, spleen, satiety, voluptuousness) that appeal only to an isolated elite. Everyday relations (family, country, work, animals) viewed through a Christian/unifying lens yield fresh and varied material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: brevity, clearness, simplicity and openness to everyone
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not bulkiness, obscurity, and complexity of form... but, on the contrary, brevity, clearness, and simplicity of expression.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms of art should be comprehensible and memorable to broad audiences (e.g., a simple story without unnecessary details, a pencil sketch that touches, a short clear melody). It is more difficult and more valuable to produce simple, clear forms than to create technically elaborate works that only a few understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's life condition: live common life and labour; avoid secure luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: “The artist of the future will live the common life of man, earning his subsistence by some kind of labour... security of maintenance is a condition most harmful to an artist’s true productiveness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True artistic feeling arises from living the ordinary human condition, including struggle for subsistence; prolonged security and luxury remove artists from natural feelings and thus diminish genuine artistic production. Artists should not be isolated professionals producing art for pay alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as transmission of experienced feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: “Art is the transmission of feeling the artist has experienced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The core measure of art's success is its capacity to convey the actual feeling the artist experienced into the feelings of others. Art is not mere craft or amusement; its value rests in authentically communicating inner perceptions to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of excellence: universality of feeling and wide diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The ideal of excellence in the future will not be the exclusiveness of feeling... but, on the contrary, its universality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excellent art is judged by how widely and deeply it transmits feeling—whether it reaches and unites diverse people—rather than by technical virtuosity or exclusivity. Works that endure across generations and affect many (folk songs, lullabies, simple jests) are especially valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of folk, children's, and simple popular forms
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the immense realm of folk-art, and children’s art—jests, proverbs, riddles, songs, dances, children’s games, and mimicry—was not esteemed a domain worthy of art.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy elevates simple popular forms (fairy-tales, little songs, lullabies, riddles, sketches, short melodies) as potentially more important and fruitful than complex elite forms (novels, symphonies, grand paintings) that merely entertain the wealthy for a time and are soon forgotten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and technique learned chiefly from life and examples, not schools
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every true artist, even now, learns his technique, chiefly, not in the schools but in life, from the examples of the great masters... such examples ... will be the best schools of technique for their successors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formal schools teach specialised complications, true technique—clearness, compression, beauty—is acquired through exposure to living examples and practice in life's conditions. Broader diffusion of good art will compensate for any loss of specialised schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ‘art for art’s sake’; align art with true science and moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy criticises art-for-art’s-sake and argues art must be guided by the religious perception of the time and by 'real science' that studies how human life should be arranged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should not be autonomous entertainment divorced from moral and social truths. It must work in concert with science (properly oriented to human well-being) to transmit truths from reason into feeling and to cultivate social virtues (brotherhood, shame of luxury and violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function: art should educate feelings to secure voluntary, joyous cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The task of art is enormous... Art should transform this perception into feeling... Art should cause violence to be set aside.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art's normative aim is to instil the feeling of brotherhood and love, making humane behaviour habitual and voluntary rather than enforced by law or coercion. Through imagined conditions and emotional training, art lays the 'rails' for moral actions in real life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of artistic importance: practical relation to human life
rubrics_metrics.description: True science and art should concern themselves with questions important for human life—education, sexual relations, land-use, treatment of animals, war, poverty—rather than mere curiosity or technical novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art (and allied science) is important insofar as it addresses and helps to improve concrete conditions of human life; works that reinforce or justify existing harmful social arrangements are condemned, whereas those that illuminate and promote humane reforms are valuable.
